snippet.title: The Real Tony Spilotro Was the Chicago Outfit’s Deadliest Enforcer
snippet.description:
He was supposed to be the Outfit’s man in Vegas. Instead, he became its biggest liability. The real Tony Spilotro made Joe Pesci’s Casino character look like a Disney villain. This is the unsanitized story Scorsese could not put on screen.

In June 1986, an Indiana farmer’s tractor blade hit something soft in a cornfield outside Enos. It was a hand. Beneath it lay Tony Spilotro and his brother Michael, beaten beyond recognition, buried in their underwear, and according to forensic evidence, still breathing when the dirt went over them. The corn cob detail Scorsese cut from Casino was real, and we tell you why.

What you will learn in this documentary:
- How a 5 foot 2 kid from Chicago’s West Side became the most feared enforcer in Las Vegas
- The vise murder that earned him his button at age 24
- The full mechanics of the Hole in the Wall Gang and how they stole over 10 million dollars in jewelry
- The exact reason the Chicago Outfit ordered his execution
- Why his affair with Geri Rosenthal sealed his fate
- The 1982 car bomb that should have killed Lefty Rosenthal but didn’t
- How Frank Cullotta’s betrayal dismantled the entire Vegas operation
- The Family Secrets trial that finally exposed who killed him

Key figures: 
Tony Spilotro, Michael Spilotro, Frank Lefty Rosenthal, Geri Rosenthal, Frank Cullotta, Joe Aiuppa, Tony Accardo, Sam DeStefano, Nicholas Calabrese, Joey Lombardo

Timeline: 
1938 birth in Chicago, 1962 M and M Murders, 1971 Vegas assignment, 1974 to 1981 Hole in the Wall Gang, October 1982 Lefty car bomb, June 14 1986 the Bensenville basement, 2007 Family Secrets trial revelations.

Why this story matters today: 
The Spilotro case ended the old skim era of Las Vegas forever and triggered the corporate takeover of the Strip. Every modern Vegas casino exists in the shadow of what happened to Tony Spilotro.

snippet.title: Goodfellas Never Showed the Brutal Murder of Theresa Ferrara
snippet.description:
Goodfellas showed the Lufthansa heist as a robbery that made Jimmy Burke’s crew rich. But it did not show the darkest part of what came after. After the money vanished, so did the people. And one of the most haunting names in that trail of blood was Theresa Ferrara.

Theresa was not a made man. She was not a robber who walked into the Lufthansa cargo terminal. She was a young Long Island woman connected to dangerous men, dangerous money, and dangerous secrets. She moved around the same world as Jimmy Burke, Henry Hill, Tommy DeSimone, Tom Monteleone, and the Lucchese-connected crew that turned the biggest cash robbery in American history into a murder spree.

On February 10, 1979, Theresa Ferrara received a phone call while she was at work. According to later accounts, she told her niece she was going out to make ten thousand dollars and would be right back. She never returned.

Months later, on May 18, 1979, a human torso washed up near Barnegat Inlet on the New Jersey shore. No head. No hands. Nothing easy to identify. Investigators eventually connected the remains to Theresa Ferrara. She was twenty-seven years old.

The official truth stopped there.

But the underworld whispers never did. Some believed Theresa knew too much about the Lufthansa money. Others believed she knew too much about a drug deal, a fake cocaine scheme, or the people laundering stolen cash. Some accounts say she may have been informing. Others point to Jimmy Burke’s growing paranoia after the robbery. Whatever the exact reason, Theresa Ferrara entered the most dangerous moment in mob history: the months after Lufthansa, when anyone connected to the money could become a loose end.

What you will learn in this documentary:
How Theresa Ferrara became connected to Jimmy Burke’s criminal world
Why the Lufthansa heist created a wave of paranoia inside the Lucchese-connected crew

snippet.title: Joe Aiello Put a Price on Capone — Then Chicago Buried Him in Bullets
snippet.description:
He thought he could outbid, outfight, and outlast Al Capone. Joe Aiello was not just another Chicago bootlegger. He was a Sicilian power player, a Unione Siciliana boss, and one of the few men reckless enough to put a price on Capone’s head. But in Prohibition Chicago, threatening Scarface was not ambition. It was a death sentence.

By the late 1920s, Chicago was no longer just a city. It was a battlefield of beer trucks, machine guns, political protection, Sicilian factions, and street empires built on blood. Capone controlled the Outfit. Joe Aiello wanted power in the Italian underworld. And between them stood the Unione Siciliana, the most important Sicilian organization in Chicago — a group that looked respectable on paper, but was tied to influence, fear, and underworld control.

Aiello wanted Capone gone.

He reportedly offered money to kill him. He plotted against him. He aligned with Capone’s enemies. He fought through proxies, assassins, and gangland alliances. But every move against Capone only made the war more dangerous. One by one, men around Aiello were killed, chased, bought, or broken. Then on October 23, 1930, Chicago finally answered him.

As Aiello stepped out near North Kolmar Avenue, gunmen opened fire from hidden positions. Thompson machine guns tore into the street. Aiello ran, stumbled, and was cut down in a storm of bullets. The man who had put a price on Capone was buried by the city Capone controlled.

What you will learn in this documentary:
How Joe Aiello rose from Sicilian immigrant to one of Chicago’s most dangerous bootleggers
Why the Unione Siciliana became a hidden prize in the Chicago underworld
How Aiello’s feud with Antonio Lombardo pulled him directly into Capone’s path
Why Aiello believed he could challenge Al Capone for power
How attempted poison plots and assassination schemes made Aiello a marked man

It was a death sentence.

And between them stood the Unione Siciliana, the most important Sicilian organization in Chicago — a group that looked respectable on paper, but was tied to influence, fear, and underworld control.

But every move against Capone only made the war more dangerous. One by one, men around Aiello were killed, chased, bought, or broken. Then on October 23, 1930, Chicago finally answered him.

As Aiello stepped out near North Kolmar Avenue, gunmen opened fire from hidden positions. Thompson machine guns tore into the street. Aiello ran, stumbled, and was cut down in a storm of bullets. The man who had put a price on Capone was buried by the city Capone controlled.

snippet.title: Vito Borelli Mocked Paul Castellano — Then the DeMeo Crew Made Him Disappear
snippet.description:
He was not a boss. He was not a rival. He was not trying to take over the Gambino family. Vito Borelli made one joke about Paul Castellano’s appearance — and in the world of Big Paul, disrespect could become a death sentence.

The insult sounded small to anyone outside the Mafia. Borelli allegedly compared Castellano to Frank Perdue, the famous poultry businessman from television commercials. But Castellano was not a man who laughed at humiliation, especially when the insult came from someone close to his daughter. To him, it was not just a joke. It was disrespect in front of family.

And Castellano did not forget.

By 1980, the order had moved through the underworld. Borelli was marked. Some accounts placed the killing in the same terrifying orbit as Roy DeMeo’s crew, the Gambino family’s most feared murder machine. Later testimony and mob reporting tied the actual hit to other powerful names, including John Gotti, Joseph Massino, and Salvatore Vitale. But the message was the same: Paul Castellano wanted Borelli gone, and the streets made sure he disappeared.

What you will learn in this documentary:
How Vito Borelli became connected to Paul Castellano’s family
Why one joke about Frank Perdue became deadly inside the Gambino world
How Castellano’s pride, image, and family authority shaped the murder order
Why disrespect toward a Mafia boss could be treated like an act of war
How Roy DeMeo’s crew became the most feared disposal machine in New York
Why the Gemini Lounge reputation still hangs over stories like Borelli’s disappearance

Why the same culture of insult, ego, and revenge eventually led to Castellano’s murder outside Sparks Steak House

snippet.title: He Made Millions for the Mafia — Then the Government Came for Him
snippet.description:
He did not need a gun in his hand to be one of the most powerful men in organized crime. Meyer Lansky made millions for the Mafia with numbers, casinos, gambling systems, offshore money, and the cold discipline of a businessman. But after decades of staying behind the violence, the government finally came for the man they believed was the mob’s financial brain.

They called him the Mob’s Accountant. But Lansky was more than a bookkeeper. He was Lucky Luciano’s partner, Bugsy Siegel’s lifelong friend, a casino architect, a gambling expert, and one of the men who helped turn organized crime from street gangs into a national syndicate. While other bosses chased headlines, Lansky built systems. While killers made bodies disappear, Lansky made money disappear.

From New York to Miami, from Havana to Las Vegas, Lansky understood one thing better than almost anyone: violence made headlines, but gambling made fortunes. He helped build casino empires, protected gambling operations, moved money across borders, and stayed rich without ever looking like a king.

But the government believed he was hiding millions.

In 1970, federal prosecutors indicted Lansky on tax evasion charges. Facing pressure, aging health problems, and the threat of prison, Lansky fled to Israel under the Law of Return. But even there, his past followed him. Israel refused to let him stay permanently. The United States wanted him back. And the man who had spent his life hiding behind other men’s crimes was forced into the spotlight.

What you will learn in this documentary:
How Meyer Lansky rose from the Lower East Side to become the Mafia’s financial mastermind
Why Lucky Luciano trusted Lansky more than almost anyone in the underworld
How the Bugs and Meyer Mob helped shape the early national crime syndicate
Why Lansky believed gambling was more powerful than street violence
How he helped build mob-connected gambling operations in New York, Florida, Cuba, and Las Vegas
Why Havana became one of Lansky’s greatest underworld projects
How Bugsy Siegel’s Las Vegas dream turned into a Mafia disaster
Why the government believed Lansky controlled a hidden fortune
How tax evasion became the weapon prosecutors used when murder and racketeering were harder to prove
Why Lansky fled to Israel in 1970
How Israeli authorities rejected his attempt to stay under the Law of Return
Why he was arrested when he returned to the United States
How prosecutors failed to prove the fortune they believed he had hidden
Why Meyer Lansky died quietly while the legend of his missing millions survived

Meyer Lansky, Lucky Luciano, Bugsy Siegel, Frank Costello, Albert Anastasia, Vito Genovese, Joe Adonis, Dutch Schultz, Arnold Rothstein, Moe Dalitz, Santo Trafficante Jr., Fulgencio Batista, Benjamin “Bugsy” Siegel, Charles “Lucky” Luciano, Hyman Roth, federal tax investigators, Israeli officials, FBI organized crime agents

snippet.title: The Real John Dillinger Was the Most Dangerous Bank Robber FBI Ever Hunted
snippet.description:
July 22, 1934. Chicago. A polite, smiling bank robber walks out of the Biograph Theater after watching Clark Gable die on screen. Ninety seconds later, John Dillinger is face down on the pavement, killed by 3 FBI bullets. But the movie Public Enemies never told you the full story.
In just 14 months, John Dillinger robbed 24 banks, escaped 2 jails, killed at least 1 police officer, and humiliated J. Edgar Hoover so badly that the entire FBI had to be reinvented to catch him. This is the real history behind the Hollywood legend.

In this deep-dive documentary, you’ll discover:
• How a 21-year-old grocery store robbery turned John Dillinger into America’s most feared bank robber
 • The exact mechanics of his $10,600 first bank job in New Carlisle, Ohio on June 10, 1933
 • How he carved a wooden gun and walked out of an “escape-proof” jail in Crown Point, Indiana on March 3, 1934
 • The disastrous Little Bohemia shootout that nearly destroyed the FBI’s reputation in April 1934
 • The truth about Anna Sage, the so-called Woman in Red who sold him out for $5,000
 • Why Melvin Purvis became a forgotten hero, and why J. Edgar Hoover made sure he stayed forgotten
 • The brutal fate of every Dillinger Gang member, from Harry Pierpont to Baby Face Nelson

Key figures covered: 
John Dillinger, Melvin Purvis, J. Edgar Hoover, Anna Sage (Ana Cumpanas), Billie Frechette, Harry Pierpont, Homer Van Meter, Baby Face Nelson, Officer William O’Malley.

Timeline: 
From his 1924 grocery store robbery to his July 22, 1934 death outside the Biograph Theater at 2433 N. Lincoln Avenue, Chicago.
This story matters today because every federal law enforcement power we take for granted, from cross-state pursuits to wiretaps to the modern FBI itself, was forged in the manhunt for one Indiana kid with a Tommy gun. Dillinger didn’t just rob banks. He rewrote the rulebook of American law enforcement.

Sources verified through FBI historical records, PBS American Experience, Britannica, and the Mob Museum archives.

snippet.title: The Real Mirtha Jung Was the Most Dangerous Woman in Blow
snippet.description:
She walked into the Medellin cocaine pipeline at twenty-four years old. She walked out of federal prison at thirty-two with a daughter on her hip and a second chance most people in that world never lived to see. This is the real story of Mirtha Calderon Jung, the Cuban-born wife of Boston George, the woman Penelope Cruz brought to the screen in the 2001 film Blow.

In this deep dive, we cut past the Hollywood gloss and into the documented record of what actually happened inside the marriage that defined one of the most explosive eras of American drug history.

What you will learn in this video:
- How Mirtha Calderon met George Jung in Colombia in the mid 1970s
- The truth about her role inside the Medellin cocaine pipeline
- The birth of their daughter Kristina Sunshine Jung in 1978
- Mirtha’s federal arrest and the 3 years she served in prison
- How she got sober behind bars and walked away clean
- The 1984 divorce that saved her life
- Why George Jung died alone in 2021 while Mirtha lived on
- The decades of silence that became her redemption

Key figures: 
George Jacob Jung (1942 to 2021), Mirtha Calderon Jung (born 1952), Kristina Sunshine Jung (born 1978), Carlos Lehder, Pablo Escobar, and the Medellin Cartel network that reshaped American drug history between 1975 and 1985.

Why this story matters today: 
Every cartel documentary focuses on the men with the planes and the guns. The wives, the daughters, the households that absorbed the real damage almost never get their chapter. Mirtha’s story is the quiet counterweight to every cocaine cowboy myth. It is the rare survival story from an era that swallowed nearly everyone it touched.

snippet.title: Natalie Wood: Der mysteriöse Tod – und ihre zwei Töchter
snippet.description:
Natalie Wood ertrank 1981 im dunklen Wasser vor Catalina Island – und ließ zwei kleine Töchter zurück. Das ist die Geschichte, was der Verlust ihrer Mutter aus Natasha und Courtney gemacht hat.

Im November 1981 verschwand der Hollywood-Star Natalie Wood während eines Bootsausflugs vor der kalifornischen Küste. Am nächsten Morgen wurde sie tot im Wasser gefunden – ausgerechnet jene Frau, die ihr ganzes Leben lang panische Angst vor dunklem Wasser hatte. Ihr Tod gilt bis heute als ungeklärt. Doch in diesem Video geht es nicht in erster Linie um den berühmten Todesfall, sondern um die beiden Mädchen, die an jenem Morgen ihre Mutter verloren: Natasha, damals elf, und Courtney, damals sieben. Wir erzählen, wer Natalie Wood als Mutter wirklich war, was in jener Nacht auf der Yacht „Splendour“ geschah, warum ihr Mann Robert Wagner später zur „person of interest“ wurde – und welchen Weg ihre beiden Töchter seitdem gegangen sind.

Sein Tod im Dezember neunzehnhundertdreiundneunzig beendete die Herrschaft des Medellín-Kartells, eröffnete jedoch den Weg für neue Gruppen wie das Cali-Kartell und den Nordküsten-Kartell. Trotz seines Untergangs blieb sein Einfluss in Kolumbien noch lange spürbar – von Gewalt und Korruption bis hin zu den Nilpferden in Hacienda Nápoles. Medellín begann sich erst nach seinem Ende zu erholen und entwickelte sich langsam von einer Brutstätte des Verbrechens zu einer modernen Großstadt.

snippet.title: The Real Johnny Martorano Was the Most Dangerous Man in Boston
snippet.description:
They called him 'The Executioner'. Johnny Martorano confessed to twenty murders across three states between 1965 and 1982. He served 12 years. He walks free today, sells real estate in suburban Massachusetts, and sat down with 60 Minutes to explain why he doesn’t consider himself a killer. Black Mass gave him four minutes of screen time. This is the rest of the story.

In this documentary you’ll learn:

- The full body count — all 20 confirmed murders, name by name, location by location
- How the FBI’s Top Echelon Informant program turned Whitey Bulger into a state-protected killer for 25 years
- The 1981 Tulsa airport-area hit on Roger Wheeler that finally cracked the gang open
- The exact moment in 1995, over a steak in a federal holding cell, when Martorano learned Whitey had been an FBI rat the entire time
- The plea deal that gave him 12 years for 20 lives — and why victims’ families call it the greatest miscarriage of justice in modern American history
- The four scenes Black Mass couldn’t put on screen

Key figures: 
John Martorano, James “Whitey” Bulger, Stephen “The Rifleman” Flemmi, Howie Winter, FBI Agent John Connolly, Roger Wheeler, John Callahan, Brian Halloran, Michael Donahue. 

Timeline: 
1940 birth through 2007 release and present day.

This story matters because the Martorano cooperation deal exposed the largest FBI corruption scandal in American history — the protection of a serial killer informant for a quarter century. It changed how the federal government runs informants. It cost the U.S. taxpayer over 100 million dollars in civil settlements paid to victims’ families. And it left a free man living comfortably in Massachusetts who confessed, under oath, to 20 homicides.

snippet.title: Joan Kennedy - Das vergessene Opfer der amerikanischen Kennedy-Dynastie
snippet.description:
Joan Kennedy war Teil der berühmtesten politischen Familie Amerikas – und doch wurde ihre Geschichte fast vergessen. Hinter dem Glanz des Namens Kennedy verbargen sich Einsamkeit, öffentlicher Druck, Verlust, Alkoholabhängigkeit und ein Leben im Schatten eines Mythos. In diesem Video geht es um Joan Bennett Kennedy und darum, warum sie als das vergessene Opfer der amerikanischen Kennedy-Dynastie gelten kann.

Wir erzählen die wahre Geschichte von Joan Kennedy: ihre Jugend, ihre Ehe mit Ted Kennedy, das Leben innerhalb der Kennedy-Familie, die Folgen von Chappaquiddick, ihre Fehlgeburten, ihre Kämpfe mit Alkohol und das jahrzehntelange Leben in einer Rolle, die sie nie selbst gewählt hatte. Dieses Video zeigt nicht nur eine berühmte Ehe, sondern das Innere einer Frau, die in einer der mächtigsten Familien Amerikas langsam zerbrach.

snippet.title: They Thought Prison Broke Vito Rizzuto — Then Montreal Started Bleeding
snippet.description:
They thought prison had broken him. They thought the Rizzuto family was finished. They thought killing his son, his father, and his closest allies while he was locked away would end the old Montreal empire forever. But when Vito Rizzuto came home, the city learned that the most dangerous thing in the Mafia was not power. It was memory.

For years, Vito Rizzuto ruled Montreal like a shadow king. He was not just a street boss. He was a broker, diplomat, international trafficker, and the man who kept Sicilians, Calabrians, bikers, street gangs, and drug networks from tearing the city apart. But in 2004, everything changed. Vito was arrested for his role in the 1981 murders of three Bonanno captains in New York. Then he was extradited to the United States, convicted, and sent to prison.

His enemies saw their chance.

While Vito was behind bars, Montreal started bleeding. His son Nick Rizzuto Jr. was shot dead in broad daylight. His brother-in-law Paolo Renda vanished without a trace. His trusted ally Agostino Cuntrera was executed. Then his father, Nicolo Rizzuto Sr., the old patriarch of the family, was killed by a sniper through his own kitchen window.

The message was clear: the Rizzuto bloodline was being erased.

But in October 2012, Vito Rizzuto came home.

What you will learn in this documentary:
How Vito Rizzuto became the most powerful Mafia boss in Canadian history
Why Montreal’s underworld depended on his ability to balance rival factions
How the 1981 Bonanno captains murders tied him to New York’s Mafia politics
Why his arrest and extradition created a deadly power vacuum in Montreal
How Nick Rizzuto Jr.’s murder signaled open season on the family
Why Paolo Renda’s disappearance struck directly at the Rizzuto inner circle
How Agostino Cuntrera’s murder weakened the family’s street command
Why Nicolo Rizzuto Sr.’s sniper killing became the most symbolic attack of the war
How Salvatore Montagna, Raynald Desjardins, and other rivals tried to reshape the city
Why Vito’s return in 2012 changed the temperature of Montreal overnight
How Joe Di Maulo, Giuseppe De Vito, Moreno Gallo, and others became part of the suspected revenge cycle
Why Montreal’s Mafia war did not end with Vito’s death

snippet.description:
En las calles de Bessemer, Alabama, un hombre construyó uno de los imperios del narcotráfico más sofisticados que el estado había visto en décadas. Su nombre era Rolando Antoine Williamson, conocido en la calle como Baldhead. Cuando México lo llamó para una reunión en Monterrey, supo exactamente lo que significaba esa invitación. Rechazarla le salvó la vida. Pero no pudo salvarlo de lo que ya estaba creciendo a sus espaldas.

Esta es la historia real de cómo se construye un imperio criminal en la sombra. Cómo un hombre joven de una ciudad olvidada del sur de Estados Unidos estudió a los que mandaban antes que él, esperó su momento, y llenó el vacío que dejó la caída de Billy 'Champ' Williams Jr., el capo que dominaba el oeste de Birmingham. Cómo Baldhead tejió una red de distribución de cocaína y heroína que movió millones de dólares durante años, operando en ese espacio perfecto entre la demanda real y la atención limitada de las agencias federales.

Pero todo imperio tiene una grieta. Y en el caso de Baldhead, esa grieta tenía voz. Una conversación grabada cuando ya era demasiado tarde para parar se convirtió en la pieza que lo derrumbó todo. No fue un operativo espectacular. No fue un tiroteo. Fue el peso silencioso de treinta y seis millones de dólares en un solo movimiento bancario y la traición que nadie vio venir desde dentro.

In this deep dive, we break down the true history behind the Paramount Pictures film (in theaters September 4, 2026) starring:
• Mark Wahlberg as Gregory "The Grim Reaper" Scarpa
• Yahya Abdul-Mateen II as a young Black FBI agent named Wayne Strider. 

The film, directed by Elegance Bratton, dramatizes Scarpa's secret 1960s trips to Mississippi, including the 1966 investigation into the firebombing murder of NAACP leader Vernon Dahmer (played by Giancarlo Esposito).

What you'll learn in this episode:
• How Gregory Scarpa became an FBI "top echelon" informant after his 1962 armed robbery arrest 
• The disputed 1964 "gun in the mouth" story tied to the Chaney, Goodman, and Schwerner case — and why former FBI agents say it wasn't Scarpa who found the bodies

snippet.title: He Tried to Kill Gaspipe Casso — Casso Made Him Beg for 3 Days
snippet.description:
He thought he had killed one of the most dangerous men in New York. But Anthony “Gaspipe” Casso survived. And when Gaspipe survived, the men who came for him did not just become targets — they became examples.

In 1986, Casso was already one of the most feared figures in the Lucchese crime family. Violent, paranoid, ambitious, and connected deep inside New York’s underworld, he had enemies everywhere. After the murder of Paul Castellano and the rise of John Gotti, old Mafia rules were breaking apart. The Genovese and Lucchese leadership wanted revenge against the Gambino faction, and the streets of New York became a hidden battlefield.

Then came the attempt on Casso’s life.

A hit team opened fire on Gaspipe while he sat in his car outside a Brooklyn restaurant. Bullets tore into him, but they did not finish the job. Casso escaped wounded, furious, and obsessed with revenge. One of the men tied to the failed hit was James “Jimmy” Hydell, a young Gambino associate who had just made the worst mistake of his life.

Because missing Gaspipe Casso was not failure.

It was a death sentence.

What followed became one of the darkest revenge stories in New York Mafia history. Casso allegedly used his secret weapons inside the NYPD: Louis Eppolito and Stephen Caracappa, the two detectives later known as the Mafia Cops. Instead of protecting the city, prosecutors said these men sold police power to the mob. They leaked names, tracked targets, staged arrests, and helped Casso hunt enemies who thought the law would protect them.

Jimmy Hydell was grabbed, taken off the street, and delivered into Gaspipe’s hands. According to later accounts, Casso wanted every name, every detail, and every answer. Hydell had tried to kill him. Now Gaspipe wanted him to understand exactly who he had failed to kill.

How Anthony “Gaspipe” Casso became one of the most violent figures in the Lucchese crime family
Why the murder of Paul Castellano helped trigger a secret war between New York Mafia factions
How the Genovese and Lucchese leadership targeted John Gotti and his allies
Why Casso became involved in the failed car-bomb plot that killed Frank DeCicco
How the attempted hit on Gaspipe turned into a nightmare for Jimmy Hydell
Why Hydell and other Gambino associates believed they could take Casso out
What happened during the Brooklyn shooting that left Casso wounded but alive
How Casso’s revenge led straight to the Mafia Cops scandal
Why Louis Eppolito and Stephen Caracappa became so valuable to the Lucchese family
How police badges were allegedly used to track, kidnap, and deliver victims to mobsters
Why Jimmy Hydell’s disappearance became one of the key pieces in the Mafia Cops case
How the wrong Nicholas Guido was murdered after police information led Casso to the wrong target
Why the Hydell story exposed the terrifying power of corruption inside law enforcement
How Gaspipe’s revenge showed the difference between killing an enemy and making an example

snippet.title: Robert Lincoln – der verfluchte Sohn eines Präsidenten
snippet.description:
Robert Todd Lincoln war dem Tod von drei US-Präsidenten zum Verwechseln nah – und trug zugleich den berühmtesten Namen Amerikas.

Er sah seinen Vater Abraham Lincoln im Ford's Theatre sterben, stand wenige Meter entfernt, als Präsident Garfield niedergeschossen wurde, und stieg in Buffalo gerade aus dem Zug, als die Nachricht vom Attentat auf Präsident McKinley kam. Drei Attentate in 36 Jahren – und jedes Mal war der Sohn Abraham Lincolns in der Nähe. Diese Dokumentation erzählt das ganze Leben von Robert Todd Lincoln: den frühen Tod seiner drei Brüder, das schwierige Verhältnis zum berühmten Vater, die Einweisung seiner Mutter Mary Todd Lincoln in eine Nervenheilanstalt, die merkwürdige Rettung durch Edwin Booth und den Verlust seines einzigen Sohnes. Die wahre Geschichte eines Mannes, der sein Leben lang versuchte, einen Namen abzulegen, den die ganze Welt kannte.
